scenes.heading: ETL
scenes.narration: ETL is a data integration pattern where data is extracted from sources, transformed into a clean shape, and then loaded into a target system.

scenes.heading: The three stages of ETL
bullets: Transform it in a separate processing layer
Load the finished data into the target
Only clean, modeled data lands in the warehouse
scenes.narration: In ETL, engineers first extract data from source systems. They then transform it in a dedicated processing layer before it reaches the destination. Only after transformation do they load the finished data into the target warehouse. As a result, the warehouse receives clean, modeled data and never the raw source form.

scenes.heading: The ETL pipeline
scenes.narration: The ETL pipeline begins by extracting data from its sources. Next it transforms that data outside the warehouse, cleaning and reshaping it. Finally it loads the polished result into the target system for analysis.

scenes.heading: ETL vs ELT

right.label: ELT
points: Warehouse stores raw and clean data

scenes.narration: In ETL, data is transformed before loading, using a separate compute layer, so the warehouse holds only clean data. In ELT, data is loaded first and transformed later using the warehouse's own power. ETL suits environments with limited warehouse compute or strict pre-load cleaning requirements.

scenes.text: ETL cleans and transforms data before loading, so only polished data reaches the warehouse.
scenes.narration: The core message is that ETL transforms data before loading it, ensuring that only clean, modeled data ever reaches the warehouse.
